source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) beat UCLA students on a text-only Raven-style task (Digit Matrices), zero-shot.
numbers: Generative answers: odds ratio 1.88 vs humans (p=0.005, CI 1.21-2.91). Multiple choice: OR 6.27 (p=2.3e-8). Humans N=40. Best human got every item right.
limits: Digit Matrices are text, not visual. Training-data leakage cannot be ruled out. Some humans beat the model.
agent_relevance: Rule induction over a clean abstract pattern is a strong base skill. Spend scaffold effort on transfer to new surface forms instead.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: On letter-string analogies (Hofstadter and Mitchell style) GPT-3 beat humans overall, mostly on problems needing no generalization.
numbers: Overall OR 1.76 (p=6.3e-5, CI 1.34-2.31). Zero-generalization problems OR 1.76 (p=0.0007). Humans N=57. Accuracy fell with number of generalizations for both (GPT-3 OR 0.51 per generalization).
limits: Later shown fragile under alphabet changes (Lewis and Mitchell 2024).
agent_relevance: Letter-string success is not evidence of general analogy. Test any analogy step in the agent on a changed surface form.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Four-term verbal analogies: GPT-3 matched or beat human reference groups, and showed human-like sensitivity to semantic content.
numbers: GPT-3 as good or better than humans on UCLA Verbal Analogy Test (humans from MTurk) and Sternberg and Nigro set (human N=20); above estimated high-school SAT average on Turney SAT analogies; within human range (numerically weaker) on Jones et al. set (human N=241).
limits: Word analogies are heavily represented in web text.
agent_relevance: Verbal relational similarity is a solved base layer; the open gap is far, structural mapping.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Story analogy (Gentner, Rattermann, Forbus style): GPT-3 picked the causally matching story in near analogies but not reliably in far analogies. Humans did both.
numbers: Humans N=54: near t(53)=21.5, far t(53)=16.7, both p<1e-22. GPT-3: near p=0.0039, far p=0.065 (not significant). Humans beat GPT-3 overall, OR 0.37 (p=0.0003). 15/54 humans right on every trial. GPT-4 pilot much better, near-perfect on near, more robust on far.
limits: GPT-4 test was a pilot through the chat interface on the same 72 problems; no GPT-4 on other tasks (no API access).
agent_relevance: The near/far gap is the weak spot for distant-source use. Far retrieval and far mapping need support, not trust.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Gick and Holyoak radiation/fortress problem: GPT-3 alone gave a wrong solution; with the general story first it found convergence; with distractor stories it failed again until told to consider the earlier stories.
numbers: Qualitative single runs. Four conditions: problem alone (fails), plus analogous source (succeeds), plus 2 distractors (fails), plus hint to use earlier stories (succeeds). Also reproduced with genie/gumball developmental materials.
quote: when prompted to consider the previous stories
limits: Not a systematic sample; no counts. The hint is the same one that rescues humans.
agent_relevance: Same noticing failure as humans: a source in context is not used unless the prompt asks. Add an explicit step: consider each stored source and say which one maps.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (analogical prompting)
finding: Analogical prompting: tell the model to recall K relevant problems itself, then solve. Beats 0-shot CoT and often matches or beats hand-written few-shot CoT.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo GSM8K 77.8% vs 5-shot CoT 76.7%. MATH 37.3% vs 34.9%. Average gain about +4% over baselines. Codeforces Acc@1: GPT-3.5 15% (knowledge plus exemplars) vs 3-shot CoT 11%; GPT-4 19% vs 17%. BIG-Bench temporal sequences 58% vs 44.8% 3-shot CoT.
quote: prompt LLMs to self-generate relevant exemplars in the context
limits: Table text was garbled in extraction; GSM8K and MATH figures are the last two rows read. Analogs are same-domain (math to math), not distant.
agent_relevance: Cheap O7-style move: ask for self-generated analogous cases before solving. Treat as a baseline, not far-analogy evidence.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (analogical prompting)
finding: Self-generated exemplars help more as the base model gets stronger; retrieved labeled exemplars help weaker models more.
numbers: GSM8K by model: text-curie-001 2-3%; text-davinci-001 about 9-11%; text-davinci-002 about 47-48%; text-davinci-003 self-generated 61% vs 5-shot retrieved 54-57% vs fixed 5-shot 50%.
limits: Scale effect read from a garbled table; single task.
agent_relevance: Analogy generation by the agent only pays if the model is strong enough to produce correct sources. Gate it on model strength.

source: Qin et al. (2024) Relevant or Random: can LLMs truly perform analogical reasoning?
finding: Counter-result to analogical prompting: on math, self-generated irrelevant examples did as well or better than relevant ones. Correctness of the self-made examples mattered, not relevance.
numbers: GSM8K/MATH (GPT-3.5) average: relevant 52.4; no instruction 55.8; random same-domain 55.7; random different-domain 55.2; random biology 54.9. GSM8K: relevant 71.5 vs random-biology 75.3. On BBH relevant won: 63.2 vs 61.9 (random same), 60.4 (random bio), 56.4 (random diff). Headline: up to +4% on GSM8K with random biological examples.
limits: GPT-3.5 main; Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-14B in an appendix also showed relevant examples worse. Task dependent: relevance helped on BBH.
agent_relevance: Gains from analogy prompts may be plain extra in-context practice. Test any analogy step against a random-source control.

source: Qin et al. (2024) Relevant or Random: can LLMs truly perform analogical reasoning?
finding: Relevance of self-generated examples was low; fixing example accuracy raised results. Fixed pre-generated example sets cost less and did as well.
numbers: Mean query-example similarity: relevant 0.48, random-same 0.25, random-diff 0.13, bio 0.09, oracle retrieval 0.64. ICLmath 56.3 and ICLbio 56.4 average vs relevant 52.4 and no-instruction 55.8. Replacing example answers with random numbers gave the worst results.
limits: One model family, two math sets. Sentence-embedding similarity may miss structural relevance.
agent_relevance: Spend checks on source correctness (verify the analog's solution) rather than closeness to the target.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Failed generality check of Webb et al.: with permuted or symbol alphabets, GPT models dropped sharply while humans stayed high.
numbers: Mean accuracy over all alphabets and problem types: humans 0.753 [0.734,0.773] (1,876 samples), GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452 (6,840 samples each). Human accuracy about flat from 0 to 20 permuted letters.
quote: the GPT models' performance declines sharply on the counterfactual set
limits: Prolific humans; Hodel and West prompt for GPT. Webb later argued the models can solve counterfactuals with code or reasoning (not opened here).
agent_relevance: Surface-form changes break LLM analogy. Test the agent on re-labelled, re-ordered problems.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Error types differ: GPT models often applied an alternative rule, humans seldom. The comprehension check was mostly passed, so failure is not just misunderstanding.
numbers: Alternate-rule share of errors: 5.81%, 22.00%, 38.59% across GPT-3, GPT-4, GPT-3.5 as ordered in the table read. Comprehension-check accuracy mostly 0.9-1.0; exception GPT-3.5 predecessor with 2 permuted letters about 0.49.
limits: Table columns partly garbled in extraction; model order inferred.
agent_relevance: Failures are rule substitution, not confusion. A step that restates the mapping and tests it on a held-out pair could catch some.

source: Stevenson, Pafford, van der Maas, Mitchell (2024) Can large language models generalize analogy solving like children can?
finding: Letter-string analogies in Latin, Greek (near transfer) and symbol (far transfer) domains. Children and adults transferred; LLMs dropped.
numbers: Mean accuracy Latin/Greek/Symbol: adults (N=62) .88/.91/.89; children (N=41) .62/.66/.67; GPT-4o .85/.63/.48; Claude-3.5 .68/.62/.46; Llama-3.1 405B .79/.74/.27; Gemma-2 27B .60/.39/.14 (54 runs each).
quote: Children and adults easily generalized their knowledge to unfamiliar domains, whereas LLMs did not.
limits: Small child sample. Narrow domain.
agent_relevance: Transfer to a distant surface domain is the LLM weak point. GPT-4o beat children in Latin and lost to them in symbols.

source: Opielka, Rosenbusch, Vijverberg, Stevenson (2024) Do LLMs solve ARC visual analogies like people do?
finding: On child-friendly ARC analogies, children and adults beat most LLMs; LLM errors copy part of the example (like young children) or combine matrices.
numbers: KidsARC-Simple mean accuracy: children 3-5y 17.2%, 6-8y 49.8%, 9-11y 73.9%, 12+ 80.4%, LLMs 33.2%. KidsARC-Concept: 6-8y 56.2%, 9-11y 74.0%, 12+ 64.8%, LLMs 11.9%. Exact copies were 76% of classified fallback errors. Humans chose the concept-based error 82% (115/141), LLMs 14% (1/7).
limits: Small item set; grids as text. Many open LLMs; GPT models best.
agent_relevance: Models fall back to copying a source when mapping fails. Add a check that the answer is not a copy of a source element.

source: Bhavya, Xiong, Zhai (2022) Analogy generation by prompting LLMs: a case study of InstructGPT
finding: InstructGPT can generate analogous concepts; quality rises with size; best prompts are precise imperatives at low temperature.
numbers: Human-rated meaningful analogies (target only): 0.3B 1.90%, 1.3B 15.61%, 6.7B 48.29%, 175B 70.05%, human reference 66.67%. With a given source: 175B 53.79% vs human 71.88%. 1.4k analogies rated; Fleiss kappa .347 and .553.
limits: US raters; moderate kappa. Meaningful is not novel or useful; may be memorized.
agent_relevance: Generating known cross-domain analogies is near human level. The open question is novel ones.

source: Bhavya, Xiong, Zhai (2022) Analogy generation by prompting LLMs: a case study of InstructGPT
finding: Giving the source in the prompt helped small models but hurt the largest; prompt wording (question vs imperative) changed results a lot.
numbers: 175B fell 70.05% to 53.79% when a source was supplied; 0.3B rose 1.90% to 8.97%; 1.3B 15.61% to 29.05%. Spelling errors cut scores about 3-7% relative.
limits: One model family.
agent_relevance: Forcing a chosen source can lower quality for strong models. Let the model choose its own sources, then filter.

source: Ding, Srinivasan, MacNeil, Chan (2023) Fluid Transformers and creative analogies
finding: GPT-3 generated 480 cross-domain analogies over 6 design problems. One-shot prompts using a Duncker radiation example beat zero-shot on usefulness and distance from the problem.
numbers: Judged potentially useful: one-shot 80% vs zero-shot 40%; few-shot 67%. Semantic similarity to problem: one-shot below 0.5, zero-shot above 0.7, few-shot 0.3. Best prompt gave about 70% unique and useful analogies.
limits: Single rater screened. Few examples tested.
agent_relevance: Zero-shot 'give an analogy' returns near-domain analogies. Show one far-analogy example and ask for distance to get distant sources.

source: Ding, Srinivasan, MacNeil, Chan (2023) Fluid Transformers and creative analogies
finding: In a human problem-reformulation task, LLM analogies were rated helpful and changed formulations; about a quarter were flagged potentially harmful.
numbers: Study 1: 110 Prolific participants kept; median helpfulness 4 of 5; 185/220 (84.09%) reformulations added problem detail; 23/220 (10.45%) rejected a prior framing; about 80% showed observable change. Study 2: upper bound 28/108 (26%) outputs flagged potentially harmful, mostly upsetting content.
limits: No no-analogy control seen in what I read. Self-rated helpfulness.
agent_relevance: Analogies mostly act by adding detail to the problem frame. Use them in the restate/reframe state, with a safety filter.

source: Yu et al. (2024) Thought Propagation: an analogical approach to complex reasoning with LLMs
finding: Thought Propagation (TP): propose analogous problems, solve them, aggregate to improve the input solution. Used inside an agent loop.
numbers: Averages over baselines: +12% absolute optimal shortest-path finding, +13% human preference in creative writing, +15% task completion in LLM-agent planning (Reflexion setup, GPT-3, 6 trials). Creative writing: 5 analogous problems and 6 plans.
limits: Analogs are rephrased or similar tasks, near not distant. Abstract-level averages; per-setting tables not copied.
agent_relevance: A working propose-solve-aggregate analogy design. Needs an equal-compute control to separate analogy from extra samples.

source: Kang et al. (2022) Augmenting scientific creativity with retrieval across knowledge domains
finding: Search tool finds papers matching a user-chosen aspect of an abstract while differing in domain. Case studies with 3 scientists.
numbers: 3 participants, interviews. Participants reported new framings and new applications; domain clusters helped sense-making.
limits: Tiny N, qualitative, no control.
agent_relevance: Retrieval that fixes the relation and varies the domain is a design for distant sources. Index stored cases by purpose, vary mechanism.

source: Yuan et al. (2024) AnalogyKB: a million-scale analogy knowledge base
finding: AnalogyKB (1.03M analogies from ConceptNet and Wikidata) helps small LMs on analogy recognition and generation; unchecked data is poor.
numbers: 1,032,040 analogies, about 97% correct on a 200-sample check. Without the check about 63% of sampled points were not analogies. Human accuracy references: E-KAR 77.8, BATS 84.85, up to 99.41 on another set; mean 78.87.
limits: Mostly word and relation analogies, not narrative or design. Partial table extraction.
agent_relevance: Large analogy stores need a filter; over half of naively mined pairs were not analogies.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: analogical reasoning on narratives
finding: Benchmark of narrative analogies with near/far analogies and near/far distractors. LLMs do near analogies, fail far ones.
numbers: Humans: 96% overall, 97.9% near, 94.1% far. Models: 57% overall, 75.0% near, 39.6% far (below random). GPT-4 zero-shot was below random on far analogies. Surface-similar distractors hurt LLMs most.
quote: even the largest ones struggle with far analogies in a zero-shot setting
limits: Proverb-based multiple choice; 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Models pick surface-similar stories over structurally similar ones. Do not rely on embedding similarity for distant retrieval.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: analogical reasoning on narratives
finding: Chain-of-thought demonstrations that first extract each story's high-level message raised far-analogy accuracy and lowered near accuracy.
numbers: Up to +30 absolute points for GPT models on far analogies vs zero-shot (2, 4 or 6 demos split near/far). Near: CoT demos still hurt vs zero-shot, less than plain few-shot. Best model reached about halfway between random and human.
limits: Per-model values are in a figure not read in detail.
agent_relevance: Abstract first: summarize each source as a one-line message, then compare. This fixes far mapping.

source: Sultan and Shahaf (2023) Life is a circus and we are the clowns: automatically finding analogies between situations and processes
finding: Interpretable pipeline (extract entities and relations, then structure-mapping style alignment) finds analogies between procedural texts.
numbers: Correct mapping 87% for procedural texts and 94% for cognitive-psychology stories (Gick and Holyoak style). Retrieval test: 79% precision at top of ranking with analogy prevalence about 3%.
limits: Pre-LLM-agent system relying on QA-SRL extraction; small annotated sets (260 annotated pairs in one evaluation).
agent_relevance: Classical structure mapping as a tool: extract relations first, then align. Candidate design for the verify step.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 showed human-like difficulty patterns on matrices: progression rules harder, more unique rules harder, spatially permuted logic harder.
numbers: Humans: progression OR 0.41 (p=0.0001), unique rules OR 0.61 (p=0.0047), spatial permutation OR 0.52. Model item difficulty correlated with human item difficulty r(30)=0.39, p=0.027.
limits: Moderate correlation. Same pattern does not prove same mechanism.
agent_relevance: Difficulty tracks relational complexity for models too, so schedule harder relational mappings with more steps or checks.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (analogical prompting)
finding: Adding a self-generated high-level knowledge step (core concepts or algorithms) before the exemplars gave extra gain on hard code tasks.
numbers: Codeforces Acc@1 GPT-3.5: exemplars only 13% vs exemplars plus knowledge 15%; GPT-4 17% vs 19%. Acc@10 GPT-4 32% vs 37%.
limits: Small absolute counts; one benchmark; single run reported.
agent_relevance: Abstract the principle first, then recall cases. Same order as schema-first analogy in cognitive studies.
